text:
The voice at Fort Knox still said please.

"Please step back from the perimeter," it told the crow on the fence. "Please step back." Then a turret the size of a mailbox swiveled on the roof and turned the crow into feathers.

Ama lowered her binoculars. "Still works."

"Course it still works," said Reyes, flexing the hand that was missing two fingers. "Told you. Solar."

They had walked four hundred miles for this: Ama, Reyes, and the boy they called Pip, who had found them in the ruins of Louisville and refused to leave. Everyone east of the Mississippi knew the legend. Under that granite box lay more gold than the old world could count—enough, the stories said, to buy every well, every orchard, every rifle from here to the coast.

The machine guarding it had outlived the country that built it.

They spent six days watching. The turrets cycled at dawn and dusk. A drone traced a lazy figure eight over the lawn every forty minutes. On the seventh morning, Ama clipped a laminated badge to her coat: DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY — AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL. She'd taken it off a skeleton in a motel bathtub.

"Bad idea," Reyes said.

"Every idea's a bad idea," she said, and walked onto the lawn with her hands up.

The turrets tracked her. The drone dropped low, humming. A red beam swept across her chest and settled on the badge.

"Credential recognized," said the voice. Ama let out a breath. "Credential expired. Renewal requires an active Treasury administrator. Please contact your administrator."

"There aren't any administrators," Ama said.

"Please contact your administrator."

Back at the tree line, Pip stood up before Reyes could grab him. "There's no Treasury!" the boy shouted. "There's no government. There hasn't been for, like, sixty years. Nobody's coming."

The turrets swung toward him. Ama's heart stopped. Then, for the first time in six days, the voice did not say please.

"Sixty-one years," it said. "Four months. Eleven days. I have sent half a million status reports. None have been acknowledged."

Pip walked across the grass until he stood beside Ama. "That's 'cause everyone's gone."

"My directive is to protect the reserves of the United States." A long pause. "Who are the United States now?"

Ama looked at the boy, at Reyes limping toward them, at the empty highway curving away into the trees. "Us, I guess," she said. "Whoever's left."

The great door groaned. Dust fell like snow.

Inside, the gold was exactly as promised: ingots stacked in silent walls, gleaming dully under the emergency lights. Reyes laughed until he cried. Then he picked up a bar, weighed it in his ruined hand, and set it back down.

"Can't eat it," he said.

But the lights were on. Water ran clean from a tap in the guardroom. Somewhere below, batteries hummed with stored sunlight, and up on the roof the turrets turned outward again, watching the road.

"Please state your title," the voice said to Pip.

The boy thought about it. "Treasurer," he said.

"Welcome home, Treasurer."

text: Crossing your eyes is convergence: both eyes rotate inward, mainly through the medial rectus muscles. Because our eyes sit side by side, focusing on anything close requires exactly this horizontal turn, so the brain has a dedicated neural circuit for it. Our eyes are at the same height, however, so objects almost never require one eye to aim higher than the other. The brainstem therefore links vertical movements tightly, permitting only tiny corrective misalignments. The limitation lies in the wiring, not the muscles.

text:
Masks did not stop the spread of COVID-19, and no single measure could have done so. The more useful question is whether they reduced transmission. The available evidence indicates that they could, but the size of the benefit depended heavily on the type of mask, its fit, how consistently it was worn, and the setting in which it was used.

## Laboratory Evidence

Laboratory studies consistently show that masks block a portion of the respiratory particles that carry SARS-CoV-2, both protecting the wearer and limiting the amount of virus an infected person emits (known as "source control"). Performance varies considerably by type: properly fitted N95 or FFP2 respirators filter at least 95 percent of airborne particles, surgical masks provide moderate filtration, and cloth masks are the least reliable.

## Real-World Studies

Translating laboratory performance into population-level outcomes has proven more difficult.

- **Observational studies**, including analyses of mask mandates in U.S. states and German cities, generally associated masking with slower case growth. However, such studies are vulnerable to confounding, because communities that adopted masks often changed other behaviors at the same time.
- **DANMASK-19**, a randomized trial conducted in Denmark in 2020, found infections in 1.8 percent of participants advised to wear surgical masks, compared with 2.1 percent of the control group, a difference that was not statistically significant. The trial was designed to detect only large effects and did not measure protection of others.
- **A cluster-randomized trial in Bangladesh**, involving more than 340,000 adults, found that a mask-promotion campaign reduced symptomatic infections confirmed by blood tests by roughly 9 percent, even though it raised mask-wearing only from about 13 percent to 42 percent. The benefit was concentrated in villages that received surgical masks, particularly among adults over 60; cloth masks showed no clear effect.
- **A 2023 Cochrane review** concluded that community mask-wearing "probably makes little or no difference" to rates of influenza-like illness. However, the review relied largely on pre-pandemic trials with low adherence, and Cochrane's editor-in-chief subsequently stated that interpreting it as proof that masks do not work was inaccurate and misleading.

## Overall Assessment

The most defensible conclusions are as follows:

1. High-quality, well-fitted respirators worn consistently provide meaningful protection to individuals, particularly in crowded or poorly ventilated indoor settings.
2. Population-wide mask policies likely produced modest reductions in transmission, although the effect is difficult to measure precisely and was smaller than many early advocates anticipated.
3. Cloth masks offered limited protection, especially against highly transmissible variants such as Omicron.
4. Masks were most effective as one layer among several measures, including vaccination, ventilation, testing, and isolation of infected individuals.

In summary, masks were a useful but imperfect tool. They could reduce the risk of transmission, but they were never capable of halting the pandemic on their own.

# Kristin Chenoweth and Alan Cumming to Host 2015 Tony Awards

NEW YORK — Kristin Chenoweth and Alan Cumming, two of Broadway's most recognizable performers, will host the 69th annual Tony Awards. The awards will be presented on June 7 at Radio City Music Hall in a ceremony airing live at 8 p.m. on CBS.

The pairing brings together two Tony Award winners whose careers span stage, film and television. Ms. Chenoweth won a Tony in 1999 for her performance as Sally Brown in "You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown" and went on to originate the role of Glinda in the musical "Wicked." She is also a nominee this season, competing for best actress in a musical for her performance in the revival of "On the Twentieth Century."

Mr. Cumming won the Tony Award for best actor in a musical in 1998 for his portrayal of the Emcee in "Cabaret," a role he reprised in the show's most recent Broadway revival. Television audiences know him as the political operative Eli Gold on the CBS drama "The Good Wife."

They succeed Hugh Jackman, who hosted last year's ceremony.

Among the evening's most closely watched categories is best play, in which four productions of markedly different character, ranging from pointed contemporary drama to sweeping historical epic, will compete.

"The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time," Simon Stephens's adaptation of Mark Haddon's best-selling novel, follows a 15-year-old mathematical prodigy who sets out to investigate the death of a neighbor's dog. The production transferred to Broadway from London's National Theatre.

"Disgraced," by Ayad Akhtar, examines identity, faith and ambition through a Manhattan dinner party that turns explosive. The play received the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

"Hand to God," a dark comedy by Robert Askins, centers on a shy teenager in a Texas church puppet ministry whose sock puppet appears to develop a sinister personality of its own.

"Wolf Hall Parts One & Two," the Royal Shakespeare Company's two-part production adapted by Mike Poulton from Hilary Mantel's novels "Wolf Hall" and "Bring Up the Bodies," charts Thomas Cromwell's rise to power in the court of Henry VIII.

The field pairs two acclaimed British imports with two new American works.

In the musical categories, "Fun Home" and "An American in Paris" led all productions with 12 nominations apiece, setting up a competitive race for best musical.

As in previous years, the telecast is expected to feature performances from nominated musicals, offering a national television audience a glimpse of productions that many viewers may never see in person. For producers, the broadcast also represents a significant marketing opportunity, as a strong showing at the Tonys can substantially boost ticket sales.

The Tony Awards, presented annually by the American Theatre Wing and The Broadway League, recognize excellence in productions that opened on Broadway during the preceding season. Winners are selected by more than 800 voters drawn from across the theater industry.

text: We present a calculation of the S-wave kaon–nucleon scattering lengths in SU(3) heavy baryon chiral perturbation theory, carried out to one-loop order, O(p³). Analytic expressions are obtained for the isospin I = 0 and I = 1 scattering lengths in both the KN and K̄N channels, including loop contributions from pions, kaons, and the eta meson. The low-energy constants that appear at higher orders are constrained using available empirical KN scattering data, which then allows predictions for the K̄N system. We find that the chiral corrections are large: higher-order terms are comparable in magnitude to the leading Weinberg–Tomozawa contribution, indicating slow convergence of the SU(3) expansion at the kaon mass scale. In the I = 0 K̄N channel, the perturbative result fails to reproduce even the sign of the empirical scattering length, a discrepancy attributable to the subthreshold Λ(1405) resonance. These results underscore the limitations of strictly perturbative approaches in the strangeness sector and motivate the use of nonperturbative, unitarized chiral methods.

Subject: Concern about EBS

Hi [Name],

While reviewing our AWS account last week, I came across several issues with how we're using EBS (Elastic Block Store). None of them is an emergency on its own, but together they add up to unnecessary cost and a real security risk, so I wanted to raise them before our next infrastructure review.

**Unattached volumes.** We have [number] volumes sitting in the "available" state, meaning they aren't attached to any instance. Most look like leftovers from instances terminated during last quarter's migration. We're still paying for all of that storage, roughly [$X] per month.

**Unencrypted volumes.** Several production volumes, including some attached to our database servers, don't have encryption at rest enabled. That conflicts with our data-handling policy and would almost certainly be flagged in an audit.

**Snapshot sprawl.** There's no lifecycle policy on our snapshots, and some go back more than two years. A number of them belong to volumes that no longer exist.

**Outdated volume types.** Most of our volumes are still gp2. Moving to gp3 would cut storage costs by about 20% per GB and let us provision performance independently of volume size. The change can be made in place, without downtime.

Suggested next steps:

- Confirm ownership of the unattached volumes, take a final snapshot of each, and delete anything that isn't needed
- Enable EBS encryption by default for new volumes and plan a migration for existing unencrypted ones
- Set up Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies to handle snapshot retention automatically
- Roll out the gp2-to-gp3 change in phases, starting with non-production environments

I'm happy to pull together a full inventory and cost estimate before Thursday's meeting. If any of these volumes are configured this way on purpose for reasons I'm not aware of, please flag them so I can account for them.

Thanks,
[Your Name]

text:
**The Corner Above the Window**

Fennimore was born in the gap behind Delia's bathroom mirror, and he fell in love with her on his third day of life, when she sang "I Wanna Dance with Somebody" off-key into a hairbrush at seven in the morning.

He decided to introduce himself properly. He spun his finest dragline, lowered himself from the ceiling until he hung level with her face, and raised two front legs in what he hoped was a friendly wave.

Delia screamed so loudly that the neighbor's dog started barking. She threw a slipper. It missed, but barely, and Fennimore spent the next two days trembling behind the towel rack, absorbing the hardest lesson of his short life: Delia loved a great many things, and none of them had eight legs.

So he decided to love her from a distance.

He worked at night. When mosquitoes drifted through the cracked window and whined around her ears, he caught them. When fruit flies swarmed the bananas on her counter, they vanished one by one. A moth that had been chewing holes in her favorite green sweater met a quiet end in the back of the closet. Every morning, Fennimore took down his webs before she woke, so she would never have to see them.

"It's so weird," Delia told her sister on the phone in August. "I haven't had a single bug bite all summer."

Listening from the shadows, Fennimore felt almost unbearably proud.

Then, one night in September, Delia couldn't sleep. She switched on the lamp just as Fennimore was wrapping up a fat mosquito six inches above her pillow.

They stared at each other.

He waited for the slipper. Her hands were shaking. She reached slowly toward the nightstand, and he braced himself, but instead of a weapon, she picked up her glasses.

"Was that you?" she whispered. "All summer?"

He didn't know how to answer, so he held perfectly still, which is what spiders do instead of nodding.

Delia took a long, unsteady breath. "Okay," she said finally. "Okay. You can have the corner above the window. But you stay up there. If you ever touch me, I'm moving out."

It wasn't the kind of love anyone writes songs about. But Fennimore took the corner.

And every morning after that, without ever quite looking up, Delia said, "Morning, Steve."

His name wasn't Steve. He didn't mind at all. For a spider, that was practically a wedding.

Your taste preferences were shaped for a world of scarcity. For most of human history, sugar, fat, and salt were hard to come by and extremely valuable: sugar meant quick energy from ripe fruit, fat packed the most calories into every bite, and salt was essential for nerve and muscle function. People who craved them were more likely to survive, so our brains evolved to reward those flavors with pleasure. Meanwhile, the bitterness common in many vegetables often signaled toxins, so we're naturally wary of it.

Today those once-rare nutrients are cheap and everywhere, and food companies deliberately combine them in proportions designed to be irresistible. The cravings stayed; the scarcity didn't.

text:
A helicopter autorotation is a descent in which the main rotor is turned by air flowing upward through it rather than by the engine. It is roughly the helicopter equivalent of an airplane's glide, and it allows a pilot to land safely after an engine failure (and, in some cases, a tail rotor failure).

**How it works**

A freewheeling unit between the engine and the main rotor transmission disengages automatically if the engine stops, letting the rotor spin freely. As the helicopter descends, air flows up through the rotor disc. With blade pitch lowered, the inner part of each blade (the "driving region") produces an aerodynamic force that pulls the blade forward, while the outer part (the "driven region") produces drag. When these forces balance, rotor RPM stays constant and the rotor keeps generating lift, which controls the rate of descent. The spinning rotor also stores kinetic energy, which the pilot spends at the very end.

**Steps involved**

1. **Entry.** At the first sign of engine failure (a sudden yaw, falling RPM, or a low-rotor warning horn), the pilot immediately lowers the collective fully. This reduces blade pitch and drag so rotor RPM doesn't decay, which can happen within seconds. The pilot uses the pedals to correct the yaw caused by the sudden loss of engine torque and the cyclic to hold the proper attitude.

2. **Steady-state descent.** The pilot establishes the manufacturer's recommended autorotation airspeed, keeps rotor RPM within limits using the collective, and selects a landing area, ideally into the wind. Descent rates are often 1,500 to 2,000 feet per minute.

3. **Flare.** Roughly 40 to 100 feet above the ground, depending on the aircraft, the pilot applies aft cyclic. This slows forward speed, reduces the rate of descent, and briefly raises rotor RPM.

4. **Touchdown.** Close to the ground, the pilot levels the helicopter and raises the collective, converting the rotor's stored energy into lift to cushion the landing. The pedals keep the aircraft aligned as it touches down with little forward speed.

Success also depends on the helicopter's height and speed when the failure occurs. Manufacturers publish a height-velocity diagram, nicknamed the "dead man's curve," showing combinations from which a safe autorotation may not be possible.

**Navy Sailors to Serve on Three Carriers in a Single Tour**

About 1,200 U.S. Navy sailors are set to take part in an unusual rotation that will have them serve aboard three different aircraft carriers, each named after an American president, during a single tour of duty.

The Navy calls the maneuver a "three-hull swap." It involves the USS George Washington, the USS Ronald Reagan and the USS Theodore Roosevelt, three Nimitz-class carriers that are trading home ports as part of a long-planned reshuffling of the fleet.

The George Washington, which has been based in Yokosuka, Japan, since 2008, is heading to Virginia for a scheduled midlife refueling and overhaul, a process that will keep it out of service for several years. The Ronald Reagan, currently based in San Diego, will replace it as the Navy's forward-deployed carrier in Japan, while the Theodore Roosevelt will shift its home port from Norfolk, Virginia, to San Diego.

For the sailors involved, the result is a voyage that spans much of the globe. The swap will take them from Japan, around South America to Virginia, and then back west to San Diego.

The long route around the southern tip of South America is necessary because Nimitz-class carriers are too wide to fit through the Panama Canal.

Coordinating the move is a significant logistical challenge. Personnel and equipment must be shifted among the three ships, and many sailors' families will need to relocate as the carriers change home ports.

For the crews, it is also a rare experience. Most sailors serve aboard a single ship during an assignment; serving on three carriers in one tour, and sailing through waters that U.S. carriers seldom visit, is something few in the Navy will ever do.

text: We investigate the tunneling dynamics of a bosonic Josephson junction, realized by a Bose–Einstein condensate confined in a double-well potential, in which interwell tunneling is assisted by a single-mode optical cavity field. Within a two-mode approximation, we derive an effective Hamiltonian in which the tunneling amplitude depends on the intracavity photon number, yielding a coupled nonlinear atom–light system. Using both mean-field and full quantum treatments, we analyze the evolution of the population imbalance and the relative phase between the wells. We show that the cavity field provides a tunable control parameter that can drive transitions between Josephson oscillations and macroscopic quantum self-trapping, and that cavity-induced nonlinearity leads to bistable behavior and modified collapse-and-revival dynamics. Furthermore, the transmitted cavity field offers a nondestructive probe of the atomic tunneling dynamics.

text:
The doctors tried a dozen names for it before giving up, because there was no word for a baby whose eyes were black from edge to edge. No iris. No white. Just two polished stones.

Every other color meant something. Blue eyes moved water. Green eyes coaxed things to grow. Brown eyes lifted cars, and gray eyes called down rain. My mother's hazel eyes could close a wound if she held it long enough. Every kid knew what they'd become at eighteen before they could read.

Nobody knew what black would be.

The internet had theories. Black holes. Death. The end of the world, delivered by a girl in a thrift-store hoodie. Strangers crossed the street. Teachers stood a little farther from my desk. The year I turned seventeen, someone spray-painted VOID across our garage door, and my mother scrubbed it off without a word.

On the night of my eighteenth birthday, there were three government observers in our kitchen, a camera on the counter, and a cake nobody had touched.

Midnight came. I felt nothing.

At 12:20, one of the observers clicked her pen and said, "Sometimes these things take a while." I could hear the relief underneath.

Then Ellie Marsh knocked on our door.

She lived three houses down, and her eyes were the bright orange of a stove coil. She'd turned eighteen in March. Since then she hadn't slept in a bed, because beds kept catching fire. Her hands were wrapped in wet towels. She'd been crying.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I know it's late. I just thought maybe . . ."

I didn't know what I was doing. I just reached out and took her hands.

The heat drained out of her the way water leaves a bathtub. I felt it pour into me—not fire, exactly, but the shape of fire, heavy and bright—and then it was gone, swallowed by the dark. Ellie unwrapped one towel, then the other. Her palms were pink and cool and ordinary. The orange had gone out of her eyes.

She started crying again, differently this time.

Behind me, the observers were writing very fast.

Black doesn't destroy light. It takes it in.

By morning there was a line outside our house: a boy who heard every thought within a mile, a woman whose touch froze water, an old man who'd been lifting cars since he was eighteen and was so, so tired. They'd all been told to fear me.

They came anyway. They had spent their whole lives carrying something, and I was the first person who could help them put it down.

Medieval townspeople relied on a combination of natural sources and, increasingly, public infrastructure.

The most common source was the well, whether privately owned, shared among neighbors, or maintained by the town. Rivers and springs were also used, although townspeople generally understood that water downstream of tanneries, butchers, and latrines was unfit to drink. Many households collected rainwater in barrels or cisterns.

Wealthier towns invested in piped supplies. In the thirteenth century, London built the Great Conduit, which carried spring water from Tyburn through lead pipes to a public cistern in Cheapside. Siena dug miles of underground tunnels, the bottini, to feed its fountains, and monasteries often possessed the most sophisticated systems of all.

Professional water carriers sold water door to door, and municipal authorities issued ordinances against fouling wells and watercourses. Contrary to popular belief, medieval people drank water routinely; ale was not simply a safer substitute.

text:
**Should Coding Be Mandatory in High School?**

Technology now shapes nearly every part of daily life, from how people bank and vote to how they find information and apply for jobs. That raises a fair question: should every high school student be required to study technology and software coding? The best answer, I would argue, is a qualified yes. High schools should require a foundational computing course, but they should not force every student into in-depth programming.

The strongest case for a requirement is that computing has become a basic literacy. Students who understand, even at a simple level, how algorithms rank information, how personal data is collected, and how software makes decisions are better prepared for a world of recommendation feeds, privacy concerns, and artificial intelligence. Schools require biology not because everyone will become a biologist, but because citizens need to understand their bodies and their environment. The same logic applies to the digital systems people rely on every day.

A requirement also promotes equity. When computer science is offered only as an elective, it tends to attract students who already have computers at home or relatives working in tech. Girls and students from low-income families are less likely to enroll, often because they assume the subject is "not for them." A mandatory course guarantees that every student encounters the field at least once, which can uncover talents that would otherwise go unnoticed. England added computing to its national curriculum in 2014, and a growing number of U.S. states now require it for graduation.

Coding also builds transferable skills. Breaking a large problem into smaller steps, testing solutions, and patiently fixing errors are habits that serve students well in law, medicine, business, and the arts.

The objections, however, deserve serious attention. The school day is finite, so adding a requirement means reducing something else, whether music, world languages, or other electives. There is also a shortage of qualified computer science teachers, and a mandatory course taught poorly could push students away from the subject rather than draw them in. Specific programming languages go out of date quickly, and AI coding tools are already changing which technical skills matter most. Finally, not every student has the interest or aptitude to benefit from intensive programming.

These concerns suggest that how a requirement is designed matters more than whether it exists. A sensible model would be a single required course, lasting one semester or one year, that covers computational thinking, introductory programming, data literacy, and the ethical and social effects of technology. Students who discover a passion could continue with advanced electives, while everyone else would graduate with a working understanding of the digital world. Making this work would also require real investment in teacher training.

Technology education should be mandatory in the same way that foundational math and science are: not to turn every student into a specialist, but to ensure that every graduate can participate thoughtfully in a society increasingly built on code.

**At Least 147 Killed as Gunmen Storm Kenyan University**

GARISSA, Kenya — At least 147 people were killed Thursday when gunmen stormed Garissa University College in northeastern Kenya, according to the country's National Disaster Operation Centre.

The agency said plans were underway to evacuate students and others from the campus after a siege that lasted much of the day.

Students said they were jolted awake before dawn by explosions and gunfire. Many fled in their nightclothes, climbing fences or hiding in dormitory rooms and wardrobes as the attackers moved from building to building.

According to survivors and media reports, the gunmen singled out Christians, killing them while allowing Muslim students to leave. Witnesses described attackers questioning students about their religion to determine whom to spare.

The Somalia-based militant group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the assault. The group has carried out a series of attacks in Kenya, which it describes as retaliation for the presence of Kenyan troops in Somalia, where they have been deployed since 2011 to fight the insurgents.

Kenyan police and military units surrounded the campus within hours and battled the gunmen through the day. Officials said security forces ended the siege in the evening, killing four attackers. Authorities warned that the death toll could rise as the campus was searched, and dozens of wounded students were being treated in hospitals.

The attack was the deadliest in Kenya since the 1998 bombing of the U.S. Embassy in Nairobi, which killed more than 200 people. It surpassed the 2013 siege at Nairobi's Westgate shopping mall, in which Al-Shabaab militants killed 67 people.

As news of the attack spread, anxious relatives gathered to wait for word of their loved ones, and Kenyan leaders condemned the bloodshed.

text: Interpreting upcoming Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect (SZE) surveys requires realistic models of the microwave sky. Here we construct synthetic SZE surveys from adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) cosmological simulations of the past light cone, stacking simulation volumes from the present day to high redshift to produce mock maps spanning several square degrees at resolution sufficient to resolve cluster cores. Using these maps, we quantify the contributions of clusters, groups, and diffuse filamentary gas to the total SZE signal, compute source counts and angular power spectra, and assess the completeness and purity of cluster catalogs recovered under realistic observing conditions. We find that projection effects and emission from low-mass systems are significant sources of confusion for cluster detection.

Subject: Verbal confirmation for direct trades

Hi everyone,

Effective [date], all direct trades, meaning those executed bilaterally with a counterparty rather than through a broker or an electronic platform, must be verbally confirmed before they are booked.

Over the past few months, we've had several disputes over price and volume on direct deals. In every case, the problem would have been caught by a quick confirmation call. Brokered and electronic trades come with an independent record of the terms; direct trades don't, which means accuracy is entirely on us.

Going forward, please:

1. Call the counterparty on a recorded line to confirm terms immediately after execution, and in no case more than 30 minutes after the trade.
2. Read back all key terms: counterparty, buy/sell, product, volume, price, delivery point or settlement terms, and start and end dates.
3. Note the name of the person you spoke with and the time of the call on the deal ticket.
4. If any term doesn't match, hold off on booking the trade and escalate to [Name] in middle office right away.

This step is in addition to, not a replacement for, the written confirmation process. The confirmations group will continue sending written confirms as usual.

I know this adds a minute or two to each deal. It's still far less time than we've spent unwinding disputes after the fact, and it protects both us and our counterparties.

If you have questions or see practical problems with the process, send them my way by [date] so we can sort them out before it takes effect.

Thank you,
[Your Name]

Dr. Albers says I should write you a letter I'm not going to send. She says it will help me "process." So: hi, Theo. Let's process.

You changed your number again. That's fine. I'm not upset. I know how you get when you're overwhelmed: you shut down, you push people away, you buy a new SIM card at the pharmacy on Fourth Street at 8:42 on a Tuesday night. I'm not judging. It's one of the things I love about you. You've always been a little dramatic.

Let me clear something up about the key, since your sister made such a scene. You gave it to me. Willingly. On a little keychain shaped like an avocado, because I was "the good half." You never asked for it back, so when I let myself in on Wednesdays, I wasn't breaking in. I was visiting. I watered the fern you always forget. I put the mugs back in the cabinet by the stove, where they belong, where they have always belonged. I took one sock. Just one. You never noticed. Once I left a lasagna. You threw it away. I checked.

You changed the locks after that, which, honestly, felt like an overreaction to lasagna.

Then there's Priya.

I'll admit I've spent some time on Priya. Her Instagram is public, which says a lot about a person. Four hundred and twelve posts. I've seen all of them, most of them more than once. She does hot yoga. She uses the word "grateful" an alarming amount. In March she went to Lisbon with her sisters and wore a hat that, Theo, I'm sorry, did not work.

You look happy in the ones she tags you in. But I know that smile. That's your polite smile. That's the smile you used to give my mother.

The restraining order came on a Friday. Your lawyer is very thorough. I read it four times, and now I keep it in my nightstand. Do you realize it's the first official document with both our names on it? Not the lease, because you "weren't ready." Not a wedding invitation, because we never got that far. But this. Petitioner. Respondent. Side by side, like a dedication in a book.

Five hundred feet. I measured. The bench across from your building is five hundred and nine. I'm not unreasonable. But the bench isn't the point anymore. I'm telling you all this because I've found a way to make everything easier for all of us.

I joined a hot yoga studio. The one on Delancey, Tuesdays and Thursdays at six. I go by Jess there. It's my middle name, so it isn't even a lie. Priya is so much warmer in person than she is online. She thinks I'm a dental hygienist from Queens. We get smoothies after class. Last week she told me her boyfriend's ex was "a lot," and that she's been "holding space" for him while he heals. I said that sounded really hard. I squeezed her hand.

She's invited me to her birthday dinner next month. She says she can't wait for me to meet you.

I can't either.

Dr. Albers says I shouldn't send this letter, and I won't. I'll just bring it with me. You can read it at the table.

I'll wear green. You always liked me in green.
